tier_reason: BitLib README's Google Benchmark table has dynamic_bitset:: and std:: (vector<bool>) rows, and every figure in claimed_speedup matches it. The benchmark code is public (bkille/BitLib/benchmark), but no compiler, flags or CPU are stated, and several ratios are above 50x. BitLib (76 stars) is not a well-known independent suite, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: shift_left (small): 13.1 ns vs std 345 ns, ~26x (derived from page data); shift_left (large): 638,896 ns vs std 105,227,752 ns, ~165x (derived from page data); count (small): 6.29 ns vs std 234 ns, ~37x (derived from page data); count (large): 365,279 ns vs std 58,934,071 ns, ~161x (derived from page data); fill (small): 4.79 ns vs std 9.15 ns, ~1.9x (derived from page data); fill (large): 429,375 ns vs std 356,517 ns, dynamic_bitset ~1.2x SLOWER (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from a third party's (bkille/BitLib) README benchmark table, not from dynamic_bitset's own repo. The companion pinam45/dynamic_bitset_benchmarks repo has no published results. BitLib's benchmark code is public (benchmark/), but no compiler, flags or CPU model is stated. Several ratios exceed 50x, so the tier is capped at C. The large-size fill is slower than std::vector<bool> (429,375 vs 356,517 ns), and set (large) is roughly tied (2.37 vs 2.39 ns).

notes: Numbers verified row by row. The wins come mostly from word-level algorithms against bit-by-bit std algorithms on vector<bool>. Metadata checked: MIT, 180 stars, last commit 2026-09-12 (active), not a fork.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The author's CodeProject Article 2 (the live URL now redirects to /lander, so I read the archived copy) benchmarks contention_free_shared_mutex against std::shared_mutex. It states CPU (Intel Xeon E5-2660 v3 2.6 GHz, 16 threads), compiler (GCC 6.3.0 on Linux; run command uses numactl) and text numbers. The benchmark code is public at bench_contfree/main.cpp, and bench_contfree/Makefile gives the flags (g++ -std=c++14 -pthread -O3).

corrections.claimed_speedup: README headline: "contention_free_shared_mutex<> - 10 X times faster than std::shared_mutex". CodeProject Article 2 (archived), 16 threads on Xeon E5-2660 v3, std::map guarded by the lock: 0% modifications 34.60 Mops (contfree_safe_ptr<map>) vs 2.44 Mops (safe_ptr<map, std::shared_mutex>), stated as 14x; 15% modifications 5.16 vs 0.74 Mops, stated as 7x. The README charts (90% update/5% insert/5% delete, 20 usec forced delay, 2x Xeon E5-2686 v4) show about 1.9 vs about 0.4 MOps at 64 threads (~5x, read approximately from the chart image) and near-parity at 16 threads or fewer.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 6.3.0 on Linux, g++ -std=c++14 -pthread -O3 (bench_contfree/Makefile). The article also offers an MSVS 2015 build, but the published run command (numactl ... ./benchmark 16) is Linux.
corrections.hardware: Article numbers: single Intel Xeon E5-2660 v3 2.6 GHz, 16 threads (numactl --cpunodebind=0). README charts: 2x Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 2.3 GHz (36 cores/72 threads).
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark from 2017-era articles. The 10x headline is a middle value: the article shows 14x at 0% writes and 7x at 15% writes, and the lock is contention-free only up to 36 threads (template parameter). Above that it acts as an exclusive lock. The README's real-app chart (20 usec delay) shows parity up to 16 threads and ~5x only at 64 threads. CodeProject's live page now redirects to a lander, so the evidence is the Wayback copy. The last commit is 2020-04-13, so the project is unmaintained.

notes: The record's C tier came from being unable to fetch the CodeProject article. The Wayback copy supplies the CPU, compiler and text numbers, and the repo supplies the code and Makefile flags, so I upgraded it to A. The benchmark measures std::map guarded by each lock, not the bare mutex. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 522 stars, not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: doc/benchmark.md has a SpinLock vs std::mutex table (MinGW GCC 11.3.0, i5-8300H) that matches the record. The benchmark code is public (tests/benchmark/b3_b5_eventqueue.cpp), but no optimization flags or build type are stated. The CMake files set only warnings, and the makefile offers both release and debug MinGW targets, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 10M events, 100 event types/listeners (doc/benchmark.md): 1 enqueue/1 process thread: SpinLock 1303 ms vs std::mutex 1824 ms (~1.4x faster, derived from page data); 1/3: 3186 vs 2989 ms (SpinLock slower); 2/2: 3049 vs 3151 ms (slightly faster); 4/4: 1659 vs 1657 ms (tie); 16/16: 1891 vs 708 ms (SpinLock ~2.7x SLOWER, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark. The doc states the CPU model and compilers but not the optimization flags or build type, so the tier is capped at C. Results are mixed: a win at 1/1 threads, a loss at 1/3, near-ties at 2/2 and 4/4, and a clear loss at 16/16. The benchmark doc itself says SpinLock is only better when threads are about equal to or fewer than cores. Single laptop CPU, benchmarked December 2023.

notes: The table is verified, including the 1/3 row the record left out, where SpinLock loses. This is a conditional win only. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the license file is Apache License 2.0, so Apache-2.0 and copyable are correct. Last commit is 2024-12-08 (stale); 1,685 stars.

tier_reason: First-party coursework numbers. The code and CPU (Apple M4 Pro) are public and stated, and CMake gives Release plus -march=native. However, the README lists only 'Clang 18 (recommended)' as a prerequisite and never says which compiler produced the numbers, so this is not A. The headline 16x is also not a hash-table-vs-std::unordered_map comparison.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README summary: std::unordered_map baseline ~112 s; Part 1 custom tables ~108 s (~3%); Part 2 column store + Unchained ~16 s; Part 3 parallel ~7 s; 'Final speedup: ~16x faster than baseline' covers the whole pipeline, including late materialization, column store and 14-core parallelism, against a single-threaded baseline. Like-for-like hash-table swaps (REPORT.md, 113 queries): row store, Cuckoo 108,366 ms vs std::unordered_map 111,923 ms (~1.03x); Column_t layout, Hopscotch 22,578 ms vs std::unordered_map 24,696 ms total (~1.09x, derived from page data) and 12,383.89 vs 14,560.06 ms hash insert+lookup (~1.18x, derived from page data); single-threaded Unchained hashtable 7,343.33 ms insert+lookup / 15,698 ms total vs Column_t std::unordered_map 14,560.06 / 24,696 ms (~2.0x / ~1.57x, derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release plus -march=native (CMakeLists.txt). The README lists 'Clang 18 (recommended)' as a prerequisite but does not state the compiler actually used.
corrections.caveats: University of Athens K23a coursework (3 students, 1 star), with no independent replication. The ~16x headline mostly comes from architecture (late materialization, column store) and 14-core parallelism against a single-threaded std::unordered_map baseline. Swapping the hash table alone gives about 3-18%, and the Unchained table about 1.6-2x single-threaded. libc++ is inferred from the macOS toolchain and is not stated. The compiler actually used is not stated.

notes: Downgraded A to C. The compiler is only 'recommended', and the 16x figure overstates the hash table's own contribution. I pointed benchmark_url to REPORT.md (Greek), which has per-hash-table insert/lookup timings. Metadata checked: MIT, 1 star, last commit 2026-08-08 (active), not a fork.

tier_reason: The README states a bare first-party ratio ('approximately 10 times faster than std::unordered_map'). No results, hardware or run data are published. The repo does contain a benchmark harness against std::unordered_map (testCYBHash.cc, test.sh), so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++17 -mbmi2 -O3 -DNDEBUG (from the repo's test.sh; not stated as the configuration behind the README's 10x figure)
corrections.caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo, so all rights are reserved by default. The speedup claim differs between the README ('approximately 10 times') and the repo description ('approximately 5-30 times'). A benchmark harness exists (testCYBHash.cc, with bench_file_unordered_map and the symbol-table benches, driven by test.sh on bundled symbol files), but no results, hardware or compiler version are published. The numbers cannot be checked without running it. It needs BMI2 (pext).

notes: The record's claim of 'no benchmark script' is wrong: test.sh and testCYBHash.cc benchmark against std::unordered_map, and I fixed the caveats. No license means usability stays 'reference'. Metadata checked: 10 stars, last commit 2025-03-14 (stale), not a fork.
